summary:
Ryazan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The sources contain no oblast-specific or Central Federal District-specific findings, so the region is assessed at the national score rather than on local evidence.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The baseline recorded in the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025; assessment updated 11 June 2025) is that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. The 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison, and participation in the designated movement carries two to six years, rising to six to ten years for organising it.

Human Rights Watch reports that between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the extremism designation: one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. A further 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, and participants in the designated movement face up to 12 years in prison.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, a national total against which the oblast must be read. No comparison with neighbouring oblasts or with the rest of the Central Federal District is available in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ryazan Oblast live under the same national statutes as visitors, but bear their consequences over years rather than at a border. Legal gender recognition and access to gender-affirming care were removed entirely in 2023, so document changes and medical transition are unavailable within the oblast as elsewhere in Russia.

Human Rights Watch records 81 people found guilty across 98 cases under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses between January 2024 and June 2025 for displaying banned symbols, alongside at least 20 people who faced criminal charges in the same period, two of whom were sentenced to prison and one of whom died by suicide in pretrial detention. Total convictions tied to the designation stood at 101 as of 30 June 2025.

Article 20.3 is an administrative offence, meaning guilt can be established without a criminal trial; the 'gay propaganda' statute likewise operates through administrative fines for a first offence and up to four years' imprisonment on repetition. Participation in the designated movement carries two to six years and organising it six to ten, while participants broadly face up to 12 years.

No specific legal protections on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exist, and same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. LGBT+ people in Russia are recognised as a particular social group under the refugee convention for the purposes of UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contain no evidence of oblast-level enforcement in Ryazan Oblast: no record of local raids, prosecutions, administrative fines or police practice specific to the region, and no data on how often article 20.3 is applied by oblast courts. The national score is applied in the absence of local evidence, not because local practice has been verified as matching the national average.

The UK Home Office country policy note contains no Central Federal District-specific findings, so any district-wide pattern is unconfirmed in the sources supplied. Whether the oblast operates any local support services, transition-related healthcare access after the 2023 ban, or LGBT community organisations is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The sources do not state whether Ryazan Oblast has issued its own regional 'propaganda' measures, which would sit in addition to the federal statutes, nor whether local officials have issued public statements on gender identity. These points are not sourced either way.

Figures from Human Rights Watch are national and are not disaggregated by region or by gender identity; the extent to which transgender people are over- or under-represented among the 101 convictions is not stated.
